KEY MESSAGE 1...A nor'easter well off the Mid-Atlantic coast will 
bring coastal impacts and hazardous marine conditions through 
about Thursday.

A closed low off the southern Mid-Atlantic coast through Tuesday 
will gradually shift north and eastward later this week. This is 
supporting surface low pressure, which is forecast to strength as it 
slowly moves north and northeastward (even meander some for a time). 
Meanwhile, strong surface high pressure from the upper Ohio Valley 
to just off the New England coast will become more centered offshore 
of Maine by midweek. These systems will result in a tightening 
pressure gradient into our area through about late Wednesday. 

This nor'easter, while remaining well offshore, will still result in 
some impacts for our area, mainly the coastal and marine areas. A 
prolonged period of strengthening north-northeast winds will push 
water toward/into the coast. Multiple rounds of coastal flooding are 
likely (see key message 2 below). Increasing seas will result in 
beach erosion in some areas, especially during times of high tide. 
For areas along the coast, wind gusts to about 35 mph are anticipated.
Inland, no impacts are anticipated given how far offshore the storm
is likely to be. No showers are currently expected even at the 
coast, given the distance this storm is forecast to be off the 
coast. This keeps the western extent of the deeper moisture and 
forcing also well east of our coastlines. Some stratocumulus however
within the north- northeast flow will get into the coastal areas
at times, especially from the central Jersey Shore to the Delaware
Beaches. The closest approach to our coast for this storm looks
to be during Wednesday. This should be the peak of the winds across
the marine areas and along the coast.

For Thursday and Friday, the storm will gradually head farther out 
to sea as an incoming system from the west picks it up. This will 
quickly lessen the marine and coastal impacts.


KEY MESSAGE 2...A prolonged period of onshore flow will lead to
multiple elevated high tide cycles this week resulting in rounds
of coastal flooding.

As the nor'easter meanders offshore through the middle of the 
week, there will be a persistent and strong north-northeast 
wind in place. This will lead to a prolonged period of onshore 
flow resulting in multiple elevated high tide cycles. Recent
forecast trends have been lower on the crests of the high tide
cycles for this event. 

The first high tide cycle of concern is currently expected to 
be Tuesday evening as spotty minor to widespread minor tidal 
flooding is forecast. A Coastal Flood Advisory remains in effect
for the Tuesday evening high tide cycle for Ocean, southeastern
Burlington, Atlantic, Cape May, Kent, and Sussex County 
Delaware. This Advisory goes from 3 PM to 9 PM Tuesday and is 
for widespread minor coastal flooding. 

The high tide cycle late Tuesday night into early Wednesday 
morning, looks to bring another round of spotty minor to 
widespread minor tidal flooding. Due to the continued forecast 
trend of lower crests with the high tide cycles, the current 
Coastal Flood Advisory was not extended to cover Tuesday night 
into early Wednesday morning's high tide cycle. However, an 
additional Coastal Flood Advisory will likely be needed for at 
least a portion of our area.

Additional coastal flood hazards will likely be needed for high
tide cycles Wednesday, and possibly Thursday, as the high tide 
cycles remain elevated. From the current forecast, Wednesday 
evening's high tide cycle continues to be the one of most 
concern with widespread minor coastal flooding. In some of the
back bays, moderate coastal flooding is possible with Wednesday
evening's high tide cycle. Beyond Wednesday evening, the 
nor'easter will gradually be moving away from the region for 
the end of the week. Another round of coastal flooding is 
possible Thursday evening with spotty minor to widespread minor 
coastal flooding. This high tide cycle is forecast to be lower 
than Wednesday evening's high tide cycle.
